overview:
“Khamemi savva jive” (often given in full as “Khamemi savva jive, savve jiva khamantu me; mitti me savva bhuesu, veram majjham na kenai”) is one of the most widely recited forgiveness formulas in Jain practice. It belongs to the cluster of prayers known as kṣamāpaṇa or pratikramaṇa mantras, which are used in daily, fortnightly, and annual rituals of repentance and introspection. The phrase is in Prakrit, the canonical language of much early Jain literature, and it encapsulates the Jain ideal of universal forgiveness, non‑violence (ahiṃsā), and friendship toward all living beings.

Literally, “khamemi” means “I forgive”, “savva jive” means “all living beings”. In the second half, “savve jiva khamantu me” means “may all living beings forgive me”, “mitti me savva bhuesu” expresses “my friendship is with all beings”, and “veram majjham na kenai” declares “I have no enmity with anyone”. Together, these lines articulate a reciprocal movement: the practitioner grants forgiveness to all beings, seeks forgiveness from all beings, affirms universal friendship, and renounces hostility. This is not limited to humans; it explicitly includes every form of life, from one‑sensed organisms to highly developed beings, reflecting the Jain doctrine that all jīvas (souls) are fundamentally equal in their capacity for liberation.

Ritually, the formula is central to pratikramaṇa, the Jain practice of reviewing one’s actions and repenting for harm done knowingly or unknowingly. Śvetāmbara communities recite it in daily devasī pratikramaṇa, in fortnightly observances, and especially on Samvatsarī, the last day of Paryuṣaṇa, when Jains ask forgiveness from all beings and from one another, often also using the phrase “Micchāmi dukkadam” (“may the evil I have done be fruitless”). Digambara communities similarly employ the verse in the context of Kṣamāvaṇī (Forgiveness Day) and Das Lakṣaṇa Parva, where forgiveness (uttama kṣamā) is celebrated as a supreme virtue. In both major traditions, the mantra functions as a liturgical crystallization of the ethical demand to cleanse oneself of anger, resentment, and violence.

Philosophically, “Khamemi savva jive” is grounded in the Jain understanding of karma and the soul. Harmful actions—physical, verbal, or mental—bind karmic particles to the soul, obscuring its innate qualities of knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. Forgiveness, both given and received, is seen as a powerful means of loosening these karmic bonds. By sincerely forgiving others and seeking their forgiveness, the practitioner weakens passions such as anger, pride, deceit, and greed, which are primary causes of karmic influx. The verse thus serves as a practical tool for progressing through the guṇasthānas (stages of spiritual development), aligning everyday conduct with the ultimate goal of mokṣa (liberation).

Theologically, the mantra reflects key Jain doctrines: ahiṃsā (non‑violence), anekāntavāda (many‑sidedness of reality), and aparigraha (non‑possessiveness). To forgive all beings is to recognize the multiplicity of perspectives and the shared vulnerability of all souls in saṃsāra. To seek forgiveness from all beings is to acknowledge one’s own fallibility and the inevitability of inadvertent harm in a world filled with living entities. The affirmation of universal friendship and the renunciation of enmity express the ideal of living without hatred, competition, or domination, which is central to Jain ethics.

Historically, the formula appears in the liturgical traditions of both Digambara and Śvetāmbara sects, though with minor variations in wording and pronunciation. It is often embedded in longer pratikramaṇa texts and manuals of kṣamāpaṇa (forgiveness), where commentators explain its meaning line by line and connect it to narratives from the lives of the Tīrthaṅkaras and exemplary monks and laypeople. Modern Jain authors and teachers frequently highlight “Khamemi savva jive” as a concise expression of Jainism’s contribution to global ethics: a call to radical non‑violence, reconciliation, and responsibility toward all forms of life.

In contemporary practice, the verse has also taken on a social and psychological dimension. Many Jains use it as a personal meditation to let go of grudges and heal relationships, sending messages of forgiveness to friends, family, and colleagues during Paryuṣaṇa or Kṣamāvaṇī. The mantra is taught to children as a foundational ethical principle and is invoked in interfaith dialogues as an example of how religious traditions can foster peace and mutual respect. While its liturgical home is within formal rituals, its spirit extends into daily life, inviting practitioners to embody forgiveness not as a momentary act but as a continuous disposition of the heart.

primary_sources.title: Kṣamāpaṇa / Pratikramaṇa Mantra (Khamemi savva jive)
primary_sources.author: Traditional Jain liturgical tradition (Digambara and Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.original_text: खमेमि सव्वे जीवे सव्वे जीवा खमंतु मे। मित्ति मे सव्व भूएसु वेरं मज्झं न केणई॥
primary_sources.transliteration: Khamemi savve jive, savve jiva khamantu me; mitti me savva bhuesu, veram majjham na kenai.
primary_sources.translation: “I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. My friendship is with all beings; I have no enmity with anyone.”
primary_sources.notes: This verse is recited in Jain pratikramaṇa (rituals of repentance) across major sects, with slight variations in pronunciation and script. It is commonly associated with Paryuṣaṇa and Samvatsarī among Śvetāmbaras and with Kṣamāvaṇī and Das Lakṣaṇa Parva among Digambaras. The language is Prakrit, reflecting the idiom of early Jain canonical texts. Commentarial traditions often gloss each word: “khamemi” (I forgive), “savve jive” (all living beings), “savve jiva khamantu me” (may all living beings forgive me), “mitti me savva bhuesu” (my friendship is with all beings), and “veram majjham na kenai” (I have no enmity with anyone). The verse is sometimes paired with the phrase “Micchāmi dukkadam” to complete the act of seeking forgiveness and nullifying past evil deeds.

misconceptions.myth: “Khamemi savva jive” is only a social custom for one festival day and has no deeper spiritual significance.
misconceptions.reality: While the verse is prominently recited on festival days like Samvatsarī and Kṣamāvaṇī, it belongs to a broader discipline of daily and periodic pratikramaṇa. In Jain doctrine, forgiveness is a central virtue that directly affects karmic bondage and spiritual progress. The mantra is intended as a sincere inner transformation—loosening anger, resentment, and violence—not merely as a polite social gesture.

misconceptions.myth: The forgiveness expressed in “Khamemi savva jive” applies only to human beings or to one’s immediate community.
misconceptions.reality: The term “savva jive” explicitly includes all living beings, from microscopic organisms to animals, plants, and humans. Jain cosmology recognizes countless forms of life, and the ethical demand of ahiṃsā extends to all of them. The mantra therefore expresses universal forgiveness and friendship, not a restricted, anthropocentric concern.

misconceptions.myth: Reciting “Khamemi savva jive” automatically erases all past karma, regardless of one’s ongoing behavior.
misconceptions.reality: Jain teachings emphasize that verbal recitation without genuine intention and ethical change has limited effect. The mantra supports karmic purification when accompanied by honest introspection, remorse, and a commitment to avoid future harm. Continued violence, deceit, or attachment will still generate new karmic bonds, even if the verse is recited frequently.

misconceptions.myth: Seeking forgiveness through “Khamemi savva jive” means passively accepting injustice or never confronting harmful behavior.
misconceptions.reality: Jain forgiveness does not require tolerating ongoing harm or abandoning ethical discernment. One may forgive the soul of the wrongdoer and renounce hatred while still taking appropriate, non‑violent steps to prevent further harm. The mantra aims to remove inner enmity and anger, not to endorse injustice or silence victims.

misconceptions.myth: The verse is sectarian and belongs only to one Jain sect or regional tradition.
misconceptions.reality: Although liturgical details differ between Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities, versions of “Khamemi savva jive” are found across major Jain traditions. Its core meaning—universal forgiveness, mutual pardon, friendship, and renunciation of enmity—is widely accepted and taught as a shared ethical ideal within Jainism.
